mixture-of-experts: A vast dim warehouse of specialised workshop stalls—each a distinct expert with its own tools and signage—stands mostly shuttered and gathering dust, while a central router like a railway switchman inspects an incoming word-token and throws only a few levers so that a tiny glowing team of stalls lights up and processes it; a towering billboard boasts the sum of every stall’s parameters as a colossal total, yet a modest energy meter beside the active stalls shows the per-token cost of a far smaller dense network, unused stalls visibly wasting floor space, and the entire unused inventory still occupying a cavernous memory vault in the background, with a faded archival plaque noting that this sparse-routing idea predates today’s chat models and became the standard way to scale language networks past the expense of keeping every neuron awake.
model-distillation: A single panoramic illustration shows a towering commercial teacher model, rendered as a gleaming branded supercomputer with neural pathways pulsing like stained-glass windows, reciting answers and softmax scores to a swarm of incoming prompts while a compact student model hunches beside it, absorbing the streams into its own smaller architecture until the knowledge visibly compresses and transfers. Around both figures swirl rivers of public books, websites, and earlier machine-generated text that have already trained every large model in existence, emphasizing that imitation of others’ outputs is ordinary. In the foreground, torn “terms of use” contracts and “no large-scale querying” clauses lie trampled as the student siphons data at industrial volume, with critics in courtroom robes shouting “copying” and defenders in lab coats pointing back at the public-text rivers. The entire scene is framed by national flags, export-control barriers, and rival superpower silhouettes racing to bootstrap the next generation, turning the laboratory into a geopolitical contest over contracts and policy rather than mere algorithm.
open-weights: A panoramic scene shows a laboratory releasing a transparent crate of glowing numerical matrices that people download onto their own laptops and servers to inspect, run and fine-tune locally, while a sealed corporate cloud on one side accepts only remote prompts and never reveals its hidden model; the crate sits as an ice-frozen public snapshot that later padlocks cannot fully retract, a towering data-centre rack dwarfs a struggling personal computer to show the hardware barrier, and unused stacks of training data and source-code volumes remain in shadow to mark the gap from full open source.
